title: Visually Guided Decoding: Gradient-Free Hard Prompt Inversion with Language Models

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The stated purpose is to generate fully interpretable, human-readable hard prompts for text-to-image models without the trial-and-error and incoherence of prior prompt inversion methods. Paper [1] discusses prompt inversion for text-to-image diffusion models but focuses on embedding inversion, which lacks interpretability and human readability. Paper [2] addresses optimizing hard prompts for generative models but does not specifically aim to eliminate trial-and-error or incoherence in prompt inversion methods. Paper [3] proposes prompt adaptation to align user input with model-preferred prompts but does not directly address the interpretability or trial-and-error issues of prompt inversion. Paper [4] explores prompt engineering guidelines but does not aim to generate interpretable hard prompts automatically. None of the prior papers explicitly share the same objective at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Visually Guided Decoding (VGD), combines an off-the-shelf LLM's token generation (text prior \( P(T) \)) with CLIP-score guidance (\( P(I|T) \)) via a noisy-channel objective \( \text{argmax } P_{\text{CLIP}}(I|T)P_{\text{LLM}}(T)^\alpha \), without requiring training. Paper [12] introduces MAGIC, a training-free framework for image-guided text generation using CLIP, which is conceptually similar in combining visual guidance with text generation. Paper [18] uses CLIP+GAN for training-free text-to-image generation, optimizing in the latent space of GANs to maximize CLIP scores, which aligns with the noisy-channel formulation. Paper [20] discusses training-free loss-based diffusion guidance using pretrained networks, which overlaps with the zero-shot conditional generation aspect of VGD. These papers collectively cover the mechanism's underlying primitive of combining visual guidance with text generation in a training-free setup.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses CLIP-I scores, BERTScore, and human preference metrics on datasets like Lexica.art and Stable Diffusion 2.1. Paper [1] evaluates prompt inversion methods using CLIP scores, which matches the benchmark family. Paper [3] uses reinforcement learning and fine-tuning to validate prompt adaptation, which involves CLIP-based metrics. Paper [18] evaluates CLIP+GAN optimization using CLIP scores, aligning with the same benchmark family. Paper [20] uses CLIP-based metrics for diffusion guidance validation. The evaluation design (CLIP-based scoring and human preference metrics) is covered by these prior works.

### Domain
The domain is text-to-image generation/prompt inversion. Papers [1], [3], [5], [7], [8], [9], [11], [15], and [18] all operate within the text-to-image generation domain, addressing various aspects of prompt optimization, adaptation, or inversion. This general application area is well-covered by prior work.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to demonstrate an efficient, model-agnostic approach for chat-interfaced image generation that serves as a practical drop-in solution. None of the prior papers explicitly share this purpose. While several papers address text-to-image generation (e.g., [1], [5], [19]), their objectives focus on improving prompt refinement, embedding inversion, or expanding prompts for diversity, rather than efficiency and model-agnostic practicality for chat-based interfaces. Papers like [11] and [15] discuss training-free methods, but their focus is on subject consistency or textual inversion, not efficiency or model-agnostic deployment.

### Mechanism
The contribution modifies only the decoding process without requiring training, ensuring compatibility across multiple LLMs and image models. Paper [11] ("Training-Free Consistent Text-to-Image Generation") describes a training-free approach that modifies the inference process for consistent subject portrayal, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism here. Similarly, [15] ("Gradient-Free Textual Inversion") introduces a training-free method for textual inversion, which aligns with the principle of modifying the decoding process without training. Both papers share the underlying primitive of training-free decoding modifications.

### Evaluation
The evaluation measures speed improvements (e.g., 7x faster than Textual Inversion, 12x faster than PEZ, >2200x faster than PH2P) and marginal performance differences across LLMs. Papers [11] and [15] also evaluate training-free methods, but their evaluation designs focus on subject consistency or inversion quality rather than speed benchmarks. However, [28] ("A Quantitative Review on Language Model Efficiency Research") explicitly evaluates efficiency improvements in generative models, including speed comparisons across methods. This matches the evaluation design here, as both use speed benchmarks to validate efficiency claims.

### Domain
The contribution operates in the text-to-image generation domain, specifically focusing on prompt inversion. Papers [1], [5], [11], [15], and [19] all work within the text-to-image generation domain, addressing various aspects like prompt refinement, embedding inversion, or training-free methods. While the specific sub-problem (efficiency and model-agnostic deployment) differs, the general application area of text-to-image generation is clearly covered.

Paper [30] (PICARD) modifies constrained auto-regressive decoding but for SQL. Paper [7] specifically uses constrained decoding of a language model for text-to-image prompt generation, which is substantively equivalent to modifying the decoding process of an LLM for image generation purposes.
